To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a pentagonal bippyramidal array of oxygens, similar in structure and ion specificity to EF-hand Ca2+ binding sites in eukaryotes, can be engineered to bind other metal ions with high specificity, including trivalent ions that are not bound by native EF-hand sites.

the EF-hand-like Ca(2+) binding site of the E. coli D-gal/D-glucose receptor has been engineered to preferentially select for other ions, including Mg(2+), Sr(2+), and Ba(2+), by varying the size and/or charge of the coordinating oxygens, and that the ion selectivity of the site is determined by the size, charge, and number of coordinating oxygens.
the cavity size of the EF-hand-like Ca(2+)-binding site in the D-galactoside permease is important for its ion selectivity and that the site can be engineered to bind other metal ions.

understanding and engineering the mechanisms used by EF-hand-like Ca(2+) binding sites to selectively bind Ca2+ and other ions.
the design and construction of a novel class of metal ion binding proteins that can be used for a variety of applications, including the development of metal ion biosensors.
the mechanisms used by EF-hand-like Ca(2+) binding sites to control specificity.

the EF-hand-like Ca(2+) binding site in the D-Galactose and Glucose receptor is a highly specific site for Ca(2+) with a selectivity of 10(6) over Na(+) and 10(3) over K(+).
the cavity size of the coordination array is the primary determinant of ion selectivity, with negative charge playing only a supporting role.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have engineered a Ca2+-binding site to bind a variety of cations, and the site can now be used for a variety of applications.

the coordination array is the primary determinant of the Ca2+ specificity of this EF-hand-like site, that the array can bind other cations in addition to Ca2+, and that the array's specificity can be engineered by changing the side chain at the axial glutamine position.

the EF-hand-like Ca(2+) binding site of the galactose/glucose sensor is highly specific for Ca(2+) over other divalent cations but can be engineered to bind other cations with similar affinities by changing the cavity size and/or charge of the coordinating array.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the coordination array can be used to control ion specificity, and the array is a key feature of the EF-hand site.
the coordination arrays in EF-hand-like sites, which are typically assumed to bind only Ca2+, can be engineered to bind other ions.
the cavity size of the coordinating array, and not the number of coordinating oxygens, is the main determinant of the ion specificity of EF-hand-like Ca(2+) binding sites.
